title: Osmosis and water potential; Active transport, bulk transport and co-transport; Digestion and absorption; Cell surface area and size limits
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX04#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX04#t1 term and clue written for the game; MB03b#t2 term and clue written for the game; EX04#t2 term and clue written for the game. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Absorption
items.clue: Small molecules cross the gut lining into the blood or lymph

items.label: Holozoic nutrition
items.clue: Feeding in which food is taken in and broken down inside the body

items.label: Percentage change
items.clue: Final mass minus initial mass, divided by initial mass, times 100.

items.label: Digestion
items.clue: Enzymes hydrolyse large, insoluble molecules into small, soluble ones

questions.stem: A dog eats meat. At which stage are the amino acids from the meat first inside the dog's body?

options.text: When the meat is swallowed and reaches the stomach
When proteases hydrolyse the meat's proteins in the gut
When the amino acids cross the gut lining into the blood
Only when muscle cells build them into the dog's own protein

questions.explanation: Absorption is the moment the products of digestion get inside. Assimilation comes later.

questions.stem: Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?

options.text: Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.
Nitrate is taken up by facilitated diffusion through channels, which use ATP to move ions across against the gradient.

questions.stem: A cube of side 1 mm has a surface area of 6 mm², a volume of 1 mm³ and a surface area-to-volume ratio of 6. The side length is increased to 4 mm. What is the new surface area-to-volume ratio?

options.text: 6, because the surface area and the volume are both multiplied by four
1.5, because the area becomes 96 mm² and the volume becomes 64 mm³
24, because a larger cube has more surface, so the ratio rises fourfold
0.67, because it compares the 64 mm³ volume with the 96 mm² surface area

questions.explanation: Area = 6 × 4² = 96 mm²; volume = 4³ = 64 mm³; ratio = 96 ÷ 64 = 1.5. Area × 16, volume × 64: the ratio falls to a quarter.

questions.stem: How do epithelial cells of the ileum absorb glucose from the lumen when the glucose concentration inside the cells is already higher than in the lumen?

options.text: Glucose diffuses in through the lipid bilayer down its own concentration gradient
A co-transporter hydrolyses ATP directly to move glucose in against its gradient
Sodium–potassium pumps carry glucose into the cell together with the potassium
A co-transporter moves glucose in with sodium ions moving down their gradient

questions.explanation: Sodium moving down its concentration gradient, kept steep by the pumps, provides the energy to move glucose into the cell against its gradient.

questions.stem: A hypothetical single-celled organism has the shape of a rectangular solid, 20 μm long, 10 μm high and 10 μm wide. What is the cell's surface area-to-volume ratio?

Shrews are among the smallest mammals. Like larger mammals, they keep their body temperature nearly constant. A shrew must eat much more food per gram of its body mass each day than a deer does. Which statement best explains this difference?

options.text: A shrew's cells are much smaller than a deer's, so each has a higher SA:V and needs more food per gram.
A shrew's small body can store only a little heat, so it must eat often to refill that store.
A shrew uses more energy in total each day than a deer does, because its rate per gram of body mass is higher.
A shrew has a higher SA:V, so it loses heat faster per gram and needs more energy per gram to replace it.

questions.stem: A human erythrocyte (red blood cell) has a volume of about 90 µm³ and a surface area of about 135 µm². A sphere with the same volume would have a surface area of about 97 µm². What do these figures show about the adaptation of the erythrocyte?

options.text: The biconcave shape gives it about 40% more room for haemoglobin than a sphere would provide.
Flattening gives it about 40% more surface than a sphere of the same volume, which speeds gas exchange.
The extra surface can only come from the erythrocyte being smaller than a typical sphere-shaped cell would be.
Its ratio of 1.5 is higher than the sphere's ratio of 1.08 because the erythrocyte is the larger of the two cells.

questions.stem: A spherical single-celled organism grows from a radius of 10 µm to a radius of 30 µm, keeping its shape. Which prediction is best supported?

options.text: Its SA:V rises to three times the original, so each unit of volume is better supplied.
Its SA:V is unchanged, because its shape has not changed.
Its surface grows ninefold, so supply now easily exceeds its larger needs.
Its SA:V falls to one third, so less surface serves each unit of volume.

questions.explanation: SA:V goes from 0.30 to 0.10 µm⁻¹. Demand grows × 27; supply surface only × 9.
